channel.title: FT – Fiction
channel.description: Fiction reviews and articles from the Financial Times.

item.title: How Sarah J Maas’s ‘sexy faeries’ helped publishing win over TikTok
item.description: As fans await next week’s release of the new ‘Court of Thorns and Roses’ story, there is no sign that romantasy’s escapism is losing its million-selling magic

item.title: Doom Painting — AK Blakemore vividly charts the Peasants’ Revolt
item.description: An intense, blow-by-blow reimagining of England’s 14th-century uprising thrills with its rich language and palpably realistic detail

item.title: May We Feed the King — a feast for the senses in a medieval court
item.description: Rebecca Perry’s Booker-shortlisted novel plays thrillingly with fact and historical fiction in this artful re-creation of the Middle Ages

item.title: Doppelgänger — a singularly clever swipe at American campus culture
item.description: Sam Riviere’s absurdist, unruly satire charts an outbreak of ‘twinning’ and artistic imitation on a creative writing course

item.title: John McGahern: A Writing Life — banned, lauded and a late success
item.description: Frank Shovlin writes a commanding biography of the Irish writer whose work won praise and condemnation for telling the truth about life and his country

item.title: The best books of the week
item.description: From Britain’s dysfunctional energy sector to novels on TV, from English German-bashing to cold war defection and how Canada should handle Trump. Plus: a family saga by Min Jin Lee, David McCloskey’s new thriller and our pick of graphic novels

item.title: London Station by David McCloskey — the Special Relationship turns dirty
item.description: A story of the CIA and MI6 spying on each other sounds very of our time, but this new thriller is marred by too much graphic detail

item.title: American Hagwon — lessons in the immigrant experience
item.description: Min Jin Lee’s new family saga follows a Korean-American clan across continents, exploring education, ambition and their pursuit of belonging

item.title: The Floating World by Ben Eastham — tale of a failed utopia
item.description: The art critic’s debut novel is a fantastically funny, satirical take on a doomsday city for the ultra-wealthy

item.title: A classic English school story and a memoir by BoJack’s cartoonist — the best new graphic novels
item.description: Paul B Rainey’s ‘Murder School’ reads like Lindsay Anderson’s ‘If . . .’ via Adrian Mole, while Lisa Hanawalt offers charming weirdness in ‘I Can’t Stop Thinking About Horses and Sex’

item.title: In One Brief Moment All Eternity — Elif Shafak gives voice to Flaubert’s women
item.description: The oft-overlooked women from the French author’s life and novels converge to weave an inventive narrative of multiple viewpoints

item.title: The Comets — condensed, bitingly efficient short fiction by Eoin McNamee
item.description: In a collection of two novellas and 15 tightly pared-down tales, the Northern Irish writer plunges the reader into a world of danger, seediness and alienation

item.title: A History of the Novel in Britain — an epic journey through the good, the bad and the unreadable
item.description: Philip Hensher’s vast survey of fiction from Dickens to Ishiguro is invigorating, obsessively well researched and amusingly nitpicky

item.title: Trouble on Paradise and the perils of escapism — the best new sci-fi books
item.description: Conflict and sickness spell danger in other worlds, the undead spread unrest in Massachusetts, a drug-induced multiversal breach, and critters bear weapons and a grudge

item.title: Perfecting the Shot — an immersive view of the act of killing
item.description: Mathias Énard’s dive into the psyche of a teenage sniper verges on the claustrophobic — but therein lies the power of this expertly translated French novel

item.title: Partita — Barbara Kingsolver’s virtuoso novel of loss, social class and music
item.description: A dazzling follow-up to ‘Demon Copperhead’ plunges us into the grief, yearning and disappointments of a once-promising pianist in rural Tennessee

item.title: Stations by Louise Kennedy — love, friendship and the complexities of youth
item.description: The ‘Trespasses’ author captures with fino dry wit the path of would-be lovers who leave 1980s Ireland for London, and the damaging legacy of conflict and family back home

item.title: Ian Rankin’s first standalone novel in decades — and other new crime books
item.description: Sara Paretsky and John Grisham move into globe-trotting criminal espionage, Anthony Quinn takes us to 1920s Soho, and we meet a Danish version of Jackson Lamb

item.title: Dodge City — Patrick deWitt’s wild, witty road trip across 1960s America
item.description: An amphetamine-fuelled, draft-dodging journey becomes a portrait of both a family and a nation in crisis

item.title: Female Life on Planet Earth — Laleh Khadivi’s stories of solidarity and resilience
item.description: The Iranian-American author’s compassionate new novel follows a daughter as she examines her deceased mother’s secret life through encounters with other women

item.title: The reading refresh everyone needs
item.description: A return to children’s fiction is a restorative, rip-roaring way to remind adult readers of the imaginative delights of books

item.title: Booker Prize 2026 — former winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart on shortlist
item.description: The six novels span genres from dystopian and historical fiction to contemporary realism and campus satire

item.title: Booker Prize 2026 — the shortlisted titles in the FT
item.description: From a post-apocalyptic tale on the coast of Kent to a meditation on the power of secrets, here are our critics’ views on four of the six works of fiction in the running for this year’s Booker Prize. The winner will be announced on November 9

item.title: The Strangers by Naomi Alderman — the monsters in the garden
item.description: The award-winning novelist of ‘The Power’ returns with a curious mix of memoir, supernatural meditation and ecological conspiracy

item.title: Interview.Hernan Diaz on his novel Ply — ‘The gesture of the book is very punkish’
item.description: The Pulitzer winner’s third novel continues his exploration of the character of America, from geographical space to capital and now technology and human connection
